claim: Mask family proteins were discovered in Drosophila to promote the activity of the transcriptional coactivator Yorkie (Yki), the sole fly homolog of mammalian YAP (YAP1) and TAZ (WWTR1).
source: Mask family proteins were discovered in Drosophila to promote the activity of the transcriptional coactivator Yorkie (Yki), the sole fly homolog of mammalian YAP (YAP1) and TAZ (WWTR1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research establishing the relationship between Mask proteins and Yorkie/YAP/TAZ.

claim: The molecular function of Mask, or its mammalian homologs Mask1 (ANKHD1) and Mask2 (ANKRD17), remains unclear.
source: The molecular function of Mask, or its mammalian homologs Mask1 (ANKHD1) and Mask2 (ANKRD17), remains unclear.
evidence: This claim represents the state of knowledge prior to the current study and is based on existing literature.

claim: Mask family proteins contain two ankyrin repeat domains that bind Yki/YAP.
source: Mask family proteins contain two ankyrin repeat domains that bind Yki/YAP as well as a conserved nuclear localisation sequence (NLS) and nuclear export sequence (NES), suggesting a role in nucleo-cytoplasmic transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior knowledge of Mask protein structure and binding properties.

claim: Mask family proteins contain a conserved nuclear localisation sequence (NLS) and nuclear export sequence (NES).
source: Mask family proteins contain two ankyrin repeat domains that bind Yki/YAP as well as a conserved nuclear localisation sequence (NLS) and nuclear export sequence (NES), suggesting a role in nucleo-cytoplasmic transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of Mask proteins shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mask acts to promote nuclear import of Yki.
source: Here we show that Mask acts to promote nuclear import of Yki, and that addition of an ectopic NLS to Yki is sufficient to bypass the requirement for Mask in Yki-driven tissue growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-4 demonstrating loss of nuclear Yki in mask mutants and rescue by NLS addition.

claim: Addition of an ectopic NLS to Yki is sufficient to bypass the requirement for Mask in Yki-driven tissue growth.
source: Here we show that Mask acts to promote nuclear import of Yki, and that addition of an ectopic NLS to Yki is sufficient to bypass the requirement for Mask in Yki-driven tissue growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing rescue of mask mutant phenotypes by Yki-NLS-HA expression.

claim: Mammalian Mask1/2 proteins promote nuclear import of YAP.
source: Mammalian Mask1/2 proteins also promote nuclear import of YAP, as well as stabilising YAP and driving formation of liquid droplets.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing reduced nuclear YAP upon Mask1/2 knockdown or knockout.

claim: Mammalian Mask1/2 proteins stabilise YAP.
source: Mammalian Mask1/2 proteins also promote nuclear import of YAP, as well as stabilising YAP and driving formation of liquid droplets.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6 showing reduced YAP protein levels upon Mask1/2 loss and increased YAP levels upon Mask1/2 overexpression.

claim: Mammalian Mask1/2 proteins drive formation of liquid droplets.
source: Mammalian Mask1/2 proteins also promote nuclear import of YAP, as well as stabilising YAP and driving formation of liquid droplets.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6C showing large liquid-like droplets containing both Mask1 and YAP upon Mask1 overexpression.

claim: Mask1/2 and YAP normally colocalise in a granular fashion in both nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: Mask1/2 and YAP normally colocalise in a granular fashion in both nucleus and cytoplasm, and are co-regulated during mechanotransduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7 showing granular colocalization of Mask and YAP proteins.

claim: Mask1/2 and YAP are co-regulated during mechanotransduction.
source: Mask1/2 and YAP normally colocalise in a granular fashion in both nucleus and cytoplasm, and are co-regulated during mechanotransduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 8 showing similar subcellular localization changes of Mask1/2 and YAP in response to mechanical cues.

claim: Yorkie (Yki) was discovered to control tissue growth in proliferating epithelia.
source: The YAP/TAZ family of oncoproteins has a single homolog in Drosophila named Yorkie (Yki) that was discovered to control tissue growth in proliferating epithelia (Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2005.

claim: YAP and TAZ have an important role in driving cell proliferation during tissue regeneration.
source: Genetic analysis of YAP and TAZ in mice is revealing an important role for both proteins in driving cell proliferation during tissue regeneration as well as during formation of several tumour types (Cai et al., 2015; Cai et al., 2010; Camargo et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2014; Dong et al., 2007; Elbediwy et al., 2016; Gruber et al., 2016; Reginensi et al., 2015; Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Vincent-Mistiaen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: YAP and TAZ have an important role in driving cell proliferation during formation of several tumour types.
source: Genetic analysis of YAP and TAZ in mice is revealing an important role for both proteins in driving cell proliferation during tissue regeneration as well as during formation of several tumour types (Cai et al., 2015; Cai et al., 2010; Camargo et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2014; Dong et al., 2007; Elbediwy et al., 2016; Gruber et al., 2016; Reginensi et al., 2015; Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Vincent-Mistiaen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Yki/YAP/TAZ function as transcriptional co-activators of the nuclear DNA binding transcription factors TEAD1-4 (named Scalloped in Drosophila).
source: Yki/YAP/TAZ were shown to function as transcriptional co-activators of the nuclear DNA binding transcription factors TEAD1-4 (named Scalloped in Drosophila) (Koontz et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Koontz et al., 2013 and Wu et al., 2008.

claim: Phosphorylation by the Hippo pathway kinase Warts/LATS on five Serine residues induces retention of Yki/YAP/TAZ in the cytoplasm by binding to 14-3-3 proteins.
source: One key mechanism regulating Yki/YAP/TAZ subcellular localisation is phosphorylation by the Hippo pathway kinase Warts/LATS on five Serine residues, which induces retention in the cytoplasm by binding to 14-3-3 proteins (Huang et al., 2005; Oh and Irvine, 2008; Oh and Irvine, 2009; Zhao et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In response to mechanical stretching/flattening of cells, Yki can translocate from the cytoplasm to the nucleus.
source: In response to mechanical stretching/flattening of cells, both Yki (Fletcher et al., 2018) and YAP/TAZ (Dupont et al., 2011; Wada et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2007) can translocate from the cytoplasm to the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fletcher et al., 2018.

claim: In response to mechanical stretching/flattening of cells, YAP/TAZ can translocate from the cytoplasm to the nucleus.
source: In response to mechanical stretching/flattening of cells, both Yki (Fletcher et al., 2018) and YAP/TAZ (Dupont et al., 2011; Wada et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2007) can translocate from the cytoplasm to the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dupont et al., 2011; Wada et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2007.

claim: Both Yki and YAP undergo dynamic and continuous nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling.
source: Both Yki (Manning et al., 2018) and YAP (Ege et al., 2018) undergo dynamic and continuous nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling which must involve specific nuclear import and export factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Manning et al., 2018 and Ege et al., 2018.

claim: Nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling of Yki/YAP must involve specific nuclear import and export factors.
source: Both Yki (Manning et al., 2018) and YAP (Ege et al., 2018) undergo dynamic and continuous nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling which must involve specific nuclear import and export factors.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the observation of dynamic shuttling.

claim: Several regulators of YAP nuclear export have been proposed.
source: Several regulators of YAP nuclear export have been proposed (Furukawa et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Furukawa et al., 2017 and Lee et al., 2018.

claim: No nuclear import factors for the Yki/YAP/TAZ family have been identified prior to this study.
source: In contrast, no nuclear import factors for the Yki/YAP/TAZ family have been identified and these proteins lack a conventional nuclear localisation sequence (NLS) (Kofler et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kofler et al., 2018 and Wang et al., 2016.

claim: Yki/YAP/TAZ proteins lack a conventional nuclear localisation sequence (NLS).
source: In contrast, no nuclear import factors for the Yki/YAP/TAZ family have been identified and these proteins lack a conventional nuclear localisation sequence (NLS) (Kofler et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kofler et al., 2018 and Wang et al., 2016.

claim: Previous work identified an essential requirement for Drosophila Mask and its mammalian homologs Mask1 (ANKHD1) and Mask2 (ANKRD17) in promoting Yki/YAP transcriptional activity.
source: Previous work identified an essential requirement for Drosophila Mask and its mammalian homologs Mask1 (ANKHD1) and Mask2 (ANKRD17) in promoting Yki/YAP transcriptional activity, but the mechanism by which Mask family proteins act has remained unclear (Dong et al., 2016; Machado-Neto et al., 2014; Sansores-Garcia et al., 2013; Sidor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dong et al., 2016; Machado-Neto et al., 2014; Sansores-Garcia et al., 2013; Sidor et al., 2013.

claim: Loss of Mask family proteins prevents nuclear import of Yki/YAP in both mammalian cells and Drosophila.
source: We find that loss of Mask family proteins prevents nuclear import of Yki/YAP in both mammalian cells and Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 1-5 showing cytoplasmic accumulation of Yki/YAP in mask mutants or upon Mask1/2 knockdown.

claim: Double conditional knockout of Mask1/ANKHD1 and Mask2/ANKRD17 in mouse intestinal organoids confirms an essential requirement for Mask proteins in YAP nuclear import and stability.
source: Double conditional knockout of Mask1/ANKHD1 and Mask2/ANKRD17 in mouse intestinal organoids, together with siRNA knockdown of these proteins in human intestinal cells, confirms an essential requirement for Mask proteins in YAP nuclear import and stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5D showing loss of YAP in Mask1/2 double knockout organoid clones.

claim: siRNA knockdown of Mask1/2 in human intestinal cells confirms an essential requirement for Mask proteins in YAP nuclear import and stability.
source: Double conditional knockout of Mask1/ANKHD1 and Mask2/ANKRD17 in mouse intestinal organoids, together with siRNA knockdown of these proteins in human intestinal cells, confirms an essential requirement for Mask proteins in YAP nuclear import and stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5C showing reduced YAP levels and nuclear localization upon Mask1/2 siRNA in Caco2 cells.

claim: Overexpression of Mask1/2 is sufficient to stabilise YAP protein levels.
source: Finally, we show that overexpression of Mask1/2 is sufficient to stabilise YAP protein levels and can also drive phase separation of YAP into liquid droplets, suggesting that colloidal phase separation may contribute to the regulation of YAP activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6A-B showing increased YAP levels upon Mask1/2 overexpression.

claim: Overexpression of Mask1/2 can drive phase separation of YAP into liquid droplets.
source: Finally, we show that overexpression of Mask1/2 is sufficient to stabilise YAP protein levels and can also drive phase separation of YAP into liquid droplets, suggesting that colloidal phase separation may contribute to the regulation of YAP activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6C showing large liquid-like droplets containing Mask1 and YAP.

claim: Colloidal phase separation may contribute to the regulation of YAP activity.
source: Finally, we show that overexpression of Mask1/2 is sufficient to stabilise YAP protein levels and can also drive phase separation of YAP into liquid droplets, suggesting that colloidal phase separation may contribute to the regulation of YAP activity.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation of liquid droplet formation.

claim: Yki-GFP is cytoplasmic at stage 10 in Drosophila ovarian follicle cell epithelium.
source: Recently, a Yki-GFP knock-in line revealed robust nuclear localisation of Yki in the mechanically stretched cells of the Drosophila ovarian follicle cell epithelium (Fletcher et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fletcher et al., 2018 and by Figure 1A showing cytoplasmic Yki-GFP at stage 10.

claim: Yki-GFP becomes strongly nuclear during stage 11 as the columnar cells are stretched mechanically in Drosophila ovarian follicle cell epithelium.
source: Recently, a Yki-GFP knock-in line revealed robust nuclear localisation of Yki in the mechanically stretched cells of the Drosophila ovarian follicle cell epithelium (Fletcher et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fletcher et al., 2018 and by Figure 1B showing nuclear Yki-GFP at stage 11.

claim: Yki-GFP is lost from the nucleus and accumulates in the cytoplasm in mask mutant cells.
source: We find that Yki-GFP is lost from the nucleus and accumulates in the cytoplasm in mask mutant cells (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-F with quantification.

claim: Mask proteins are required for normal nuclear localisation of Yki.
source: These findings indicate that Mask proteins are required for normal nuclear localisation of Yki.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing cytoplasmic accumulation of Yki in mask mutants.

claim: Mask has no direct transcriptional activation function in a GAL4 reporter assay.
source: We began by examining whether Mask family proteins have a role in regulating the subcellular localisation of Yki, as we were unable to identify a direct transcriptional activation function for Mask in a GAL4 reporter assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clones of follicle cells homozygous for the mask∆NLS allele show a strong decrease in nuclear Yki-GFP and a corresponding increase in the level of cytoplasmic Yki-GFP.
source: Consistent with a role for Mask in nuclear import, clones of follicle cells homozygous for the mask∆NLS allele show a strong decrease in nuclear Yki-GFP and a corresponding increase in the level of cytoplasmic Yki-GFP (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-D with quantification.

claim: The NLS motif in Mask is essential for Mask function in vivo.
source: These results demonstrate the essential requirement for the NLS motif in Mask function and support a key role for Mask in Yki nuclear import.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that mask∆NLS mutants phenocopy mask null mutants.

claim: The mask∆NLS allele is homozygous lethal.
source: To test whether this NLS is required for the function of Mask in vivo, we generated a mask CRISPR-knockin lacking the NLS motif (mask∆NLS), which was homozygous lethal but showed normal expression of the mutant protein and localisation to the cytoplasm in clones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observation of the mask∆NLS allele.

claim: The mask∆NLS mutant protein shows normal expression and localisation to the cytoplasm in clones.
source: To test whether this NLS is required for the function of Mask in vivo, we generated a mask CRISPR-knockin lacking the NLS motif (mask∆NLS), which was homozygous lethal but showed normal expression of the mutant protein and localisation to the cytoplasm in clones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Yki is known to be primarily cytoplasmic in the developing wing.
source: Yki is known to be primarily cytoplasmic in the developing wing, which is composed of densely packed columnar epithelial cells (Oh and Irvine, 2008) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Oh and Irvine, 2008 and by Figure 3A.

claim: Clones overexpressing Yki require Mask in order to drive cell proliferation in the wing.
source: Since clones overexpressing Yki (MARCM clones expressing tub.Gal4 UAS.Yki) were shown to require Mask in order to drive cell proliferation in the wing (Sidor et al., 2013), we examined whether Mask affects the nuclear localisation of overexpressed Yki.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sidor et al., 2013.

claim: Overexpressed Yki is readily detected in both nucleus and cytoplasm in control MARCM clones.
source: We find that overexpressed Yki is readily detected in both nucleus and cytoplasm in control MARCM clones, but not in mask mutant MARCM clones, where the level of nuclear Yki is reduced relative to the level of Yki in the cytoplasm (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In mask mutant MARCM clones, the level of nuclear Yki is reduced relative to the level of Yki in the cytoplasm.
source: We find that overexpressed Yki is readily detected in both nucleus and cytoplasm in control MARCM clones, but not in mask mutant MARCM clones, where the level of nuclear Yki is reduced relative to the level of Yki in the cytoplasm (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Silencing of Mask expression by RNAi in the peripodial epithelium prevents the normally strongly nuclear Yki-GFP localisation.
source: We find that silencing of Mask expression by RNAi in the peripodial epithelium with Ubx.Gal4, prevents the normally strongly nuclear Yki-GFP localisation in these cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mask is required for the nuclear localisation of both endogenous and overexpressed Yki in the developing wing of Drosophila.
source: These results confirm that Mask is required for the nuclear localisation of both endogenous and overexpressed Yki in the developing wing of Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: MARCM clones expressing Yki-NLS-HA are able to restore both nuclear localisation of Yki and cell proliferation in mask mutant cells.
source: We confirm that MARCM clones expressing tub.Gal4 UAS.Yki-NLS-HA are able to restore both nuclear localisation of Yki and cell proliferation in mask mutant cells (Figure 4A–G; Sidor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-G.

claim: Yki-NLS-HA is still mildly less nuclear and more cytoplasmic when expressed in mask mutant cells compared to wild-type cells.
source: We note that even Yki-NLS-HA is still mildly less nuclear and more cytoplasmic when expressed in mask mutant cells compared to wild-type cells, and that this may therefore explain the mild difference in growth between these two types of clones (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: Linkage of a nuclear localisation sequence to Yki can largely bypass the requirement for mask in Yki-driven cell proliferation in vivo.
source: Thus, linkage of a nuclear localisation sequence to Yki can largely bypass the requirement for mask in Yki-driven cell proliferation in vivo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 4 showing rescue of mask mutant phenotypes by Yki-NLS-HA.

claim: The primary function of Mask is to promote nuclear localisation of Yki in Drosophila.
source: These results indicate that the primary function of Mask is to promote nuclear localisation of Yki in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that addition of an NLS to Yki bypasses the requirement for Mask.

claim: Silencing of Mask1 (ANKHD1) is sufficient to reduce both nuclear localisation of YAP and total YAP levels in human HEK293T cells.
source: In both cases, silencing of Mask1 (ANKHD1) was sufficient to reduce both nuclear localisation of YAP and total YAP levels, as measured by immunostaining or western blotting of cell lysates (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Silencing of Mask1 (ANKHD1) is sufficient to reduce both nuclear localisation of YAP and total YAP levels in human Caco2 cells.
source: In both cases, silencing of Mask1 (ANKHD1) was sufficient to reduce both nuclear localisation of YAP and total YAP levels, as measured by immunostaining or western blotting of cell lysates (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Double siRNA against Mask1/2 causes apoptosis of transfected cells.
source: Notably, double siRNA against Mask1/2 causes apoptosis of transfected cells, indicating that the two proteins act redundantly (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mask1 and Mask2 act redundantly.
source: Notably, double siRNA against Mask1/2 causes apoptosis of transfected cells, indicating that the two proteins act redundantly (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that double knockdown causes cell death.

claim: Clonal deletion of Mask1/2 in intestinal organoids results in a strong reduction in YAP levels compared to surrounding wild-type cells.
source: Clonal deletion of Mask1/2 resulted in a strong reduction in YAP levels compared to surrounding wild-type cells (Figure 5D) and clone sizes were typically only 1–2 cells, with cells frequently undergoing extrusion from the epithelium and death (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mask1/2 double knockout clone sizes in intestinal organoids are typically only 1–2 cells.
source: Clonal deletion of Mask1/2 resulted in a strong reduction in YAP levels compared to surrounding wild-type cells (Figure 5D) and clone sizes were typically only 1–2 cells, with cells frequently undergoing extrusion from the epithelium and death (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mask1/2 double knockout cells in intestinal organoids frequently undergo extrusion from the epithelium and death.
source: Clonal deletion of Mask1/2 resulted in a strong reduction in YAP levels compared to surrounding wild-type cells (Figure 5D) and clone sizes were typically only 1–2 cells, with cells frequently undergoing extrusion from the epithelium and death (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mammalian Mask1/2 have a conserved function in nuclear import of YAP.
source: These findings show that mammalian Mask1/2 have a conserved function in nuclear import of YAP but are additionally required to stabilise the YAP protein.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced nuclear YAP upon Mask1/2 loss.

claim: Mammalian Mask1/2 are additionally required to stabilise the YAP protein.
source: These findings show that mammalian Mask1/2 have a conserved function in nuclear import of YAP but are additionally required to stabilise the YAP protein.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced total YAP levels upon Mask1/2 loss.

claim: Mask1 siRNA has a similar effect on TAZ localisation as on YAP.
source: We find a similar effect of Mask1 siRNA on TAZ localisation (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Overexpression of either Mask1 or Mask2 causes strong stabilisation of YAP protein levels in Caco2 cells.
source: We find that overexpression of either Mask1 or Mask2 caused strong stabilisation of YAP protein levels in Caco2 cells (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Overexpression of Mask1 in HEK293T cells causes formation of abnormally large droplets containing both Mask1 and YAP proteins.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of Mask1 in HEK293T cells, which are known to generate high levels of expression, caused formation of abnormally large droplets containing both Mask1 and YAP proteins (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mask proteins may cluster/polymerise YAP to drive colloidal phase separation.
source: We speculate that Mask proteins may cluster/polymerise YAP to drive colloidal phase separation – a classic mechanism of cellular compartmentalisation (Hardy, 1899; Iborra, 2007; Walter and Brooks, 1995; Wilson, 1899).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation of droplet formation and citations to prior work on phase separation.

claim: Cells expressing GFP-tagged YAP can exhibit colloidal phase separation and formation of YAP liquid droplets in both nucleus and cytoplasm after treatment with 25% PEG to induce macromolecular crowding.
source: Recent work has shown that cells expressing GFP-tagged YAP can exhibit colloidal phase separation and formation of YAP liquid droplets in both nucleus and cytoplasm after treatment with 25% PEG to induce macromolecular crowding (Cai et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cai et al., 2018.

claim: Endogenous YAP may phase separate when it becomes stabilised and concentrated by clustering with Mask family proteins.
source: Our findings suggest that endogenous YAP may also phase separate when it becomes stabilised and concentrated by clustering with Mask family proteins.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation of droplet formation with Mask overexpression.

claim: Yki-GFP localises to intracellular granules in either the nucleus and cytoplasm of follicle cells.
source: Yki-GFP localises to intracellular granules in either the nucleus and cytoplasm of follicle cells or cultured Drosophila S2 cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Yki-GFP localises to intracellular granules in cultured Drosophila S2 cells.
source: Yki-GFP localises to intracellular granules in either the nucleus and cytoplasm of follicle cells or cultured Drosophila S2 cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Antibody staining for Yki and Mask reveals co-localisation in the same intracellular granules in Drosophila S2 cells.
source: Similarly, antibody staining for Yki and Mask reveals co-localisation in the same intracellular granules in Drosophila S2 cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In human cells in culture, immunostaining for YAP and Mask1 reveals a similarly granular pattern in both cytoplasm and nucleus.
source: In human cells in culture, immunostaining for YAP and Mask1 reveals a similarly granular pattern in both cytoplasm and nucleus (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Endogenous Yki/YAP and Mask proteins co-localise and may cluster/polymerise to form intracellular granules (or 'hubs').
source: These findings indicate that endogenous Yki/YAP and Mask proteins co-localise and may cluster/polymerise to form intracellular granules (or 'hubs') as they interact with cytoplasmic 14-3-3 or nuclear TEAD (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of granular colocalization and is speculative regarding clustering/polymerization.

claim: Human Mask1/2 proteins can relocalise with YAP from the cytoplasm to the nucleus of cultured human cells in a density-dependent fashion.
source: We previously showed that human Mask1/2 proteins can relocalise with YAP from the cytoplasm to the nucleus of cultured human cells in a density-dependent fashion (Sidor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sidor et al., 2013.

claim: Integrin signalling via Src family kinases is the primary mechanism of YAP mechano-regulation in cultured human cells.
source: We later found that integrin signalling via Src family kinases is the primary mechanism of YAP mechano-regulation in these cells and is crucial to regulate wound healing (Elbediwy et al., 2018; Elbediwy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Elbediwy et al., 2018 and Elbediwy et al., 2016.

claim: Integrin signalling via Src family kinases is crucial to regulate wound healing.
source: We later found that integrin signalling via Src family kinases is the primary mechanism of YAP mechano-regulation in these cells and is crucial to regulate wound healing (Elbediwy et al., 2018; Elbediwy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Elbediwy et al., 2018 and Elbediwy et al., 2016.

claim: Alterations in the localisation of Mask1/2 and YAP in response to loss of integrin adhesions, mechanical forces, or Src kinase activity are the same.
source: In all cases, alterations in the localisation of Mask1/2 and YAP before and after treatment were the same, suggesting that binding of Mask1/2 to YAP determines its localisation (8A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: Binding of Mask1/2 to YAP determines YAP localisation.
source: In all cases, alterations in the localisation of Mask1/2 and YAP before and after treatment were the same, suggesting that binding of Mask1/2 to YAP determines its localisation (8A-C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Mask1/2 and YAP colocalize under various conditions.

claim: YAP (and TAZ) have a physiological role in skin wound healing.
source: Finally, we previously identified a physiological role for YAP (and TAZ) in skin wound healing, which causes YAP to localise to the nucleus in leading edge skin epithelial cells (Elbediwy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Elbediwy et al., 2016.

claim: Skin wound healing causes YAP to localise to the nucleus in leading edge skin epithelial cells.
source: Finally, we previously identified a physiological role for YAP (and TAZ) in skin wound healing, which causes YAP to localise to the nucleus in leading edge skin epithelial cells (Elbediwy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Elbediwy et al., 2016.

claim: Mask1/2 are similarly nuclear localised during skin wound healing.
source: Mask1/2 are similarly nuclear localised during skin wound healing (Figure 8D), supporting the notion that these proteins are co-regulated in response to both mechanical cues and tissue damage in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Mask1/2 and YAP are co-regulated in response to both mechanical cues and tissue damage in vitro and in vivo.
source: Mask1/2 are similarly nuclear localised during skin wound healing (Figure 8D), supporting the notion that these proteins are co-regulated in response to both mechanical cues and tissue damage in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Mask1/2 and YAP show similar localization changes in response to various stimuli.

claim: Dynamic and continuous nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling of both Yki and YAP is well established.
source: Dynamic and continuous nucleo-cytoplasmic shutting of both Yki and YAP is well established (Ege et al., 2018; Manning et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ege et al., 2018 and Manning et al., 2018.

claim: Dynamic shuttling enables the subcellular localisation of the bulk of Yki/YAP protein to be governed simply by the availability of binding partners such as cytoplasmic 14-3-3 proteins or nuclear Sd/TEAD.
source: Dynamic shutting enables the subcellular localisation of the bulk of Yki/YAP protein to be governed simply by the availability of binding partners such as cytoplasmic 14-3-3 proteins or nuclear Sd/TEAD.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the established mechanism of Yki/YAP regulation.

claim: Shuttling enables Hippo signalling to control bulk Yki/YAP subcellular localisation by regulating phosphorylation of Yki/YAP and thus its binding to 14-3-3 proteins.
source: Indeed, shuttling enables Hippo signalling to control bulk Yki/YAP subcellular localisation by regulating phosphorylation of Yki/YAP and thus its binding to 14-3-3 proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the established mechanism of Hippo pathway regulation.

claim: In the absence of a Hippo signal, unphosphorylated Yki/YAP binds primarily to nuclear Sd/TEAD and thus adopts a bulk nuclear localisation while maintaining shuttling to allow continuous sensing of Hippo activity in the cytoplasm.
source: In the absence of a Hippo signal, unphosphorylated Yki/YAP binds primarily to nuclear Sd/TEAD and thus adopts a bulk nuclear localisation while maintaining shuttling to allow continuous sensing of Hippo activity in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the established mechanism of Hippo pathway regulation.

claim: The canonical nuclear localisation signal (NLS) in the Drosophila Mask protein is conserved in mammalian Mask1 (ANKHD1) and Mask2 (ANKRD17).
source: We have established the essential requirement for the canonical nuclear localisation signal (NLS) in the Drosophila Mask protein, which is conserved in mammalian Mask1 (ANKHD1) and Mask2 (ANKRD17).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the requirement for the NLS and by sequence conservation shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Deletion of the Mask NLS by CRISPR knockin caused accumulation of Yki-GFP within mutant clones of cells.
source: Deletion of the Mask NLS by CRISPR knockin caused accumulation of Yki-GFP within mutant clones of cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Attachment of an ectopic NLS to Yki was sufficient to bypass the requirement for Mask in Yki-dependent cell proliferation and tissue growth.
source: Furthermore, attachment of an ectopic NLS to Yki was sufficient to bypass the requirement for Mask in Yki-dependent cell proliferation and tissue growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Human Mask1 is required for driving YAP to the nucleus in human cells.
source: Finally, our results demonstrated a conserved requirement for human Mask1 in driving YAP to the nucleus in human cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Non-canonical 'RaDAR' nuclear import motifs that bind RanGDP within the ankyrin repeat domains of Mask family proteins may contribute to nuclear import.
source: Although the above findings demonstrate the primacy of the Mask NLS in mediating nuclear import, it is possible that non-canonical 'RaDAR' nuclear import motifs that bind RanGDP within the ankyrin repeat domains of Mask family proteins may also contribute, although the corresponding residues in Mask proteins are not strongly hydrophobic so may only function weakly, if at all (Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citation to Lu et al., 2014 and sequence analysis.

claim: Importin-alpha binding non-canonical nuclear import motifs within Yki may contribute to import.
source: Furthermore, it is possible that Importin-alpha binding non-canonical nuclear import motifs within Yki (Wang et al., 2016) and a Ran-independent nuclear import sequence in YAP/TAZ (Kofler et al., 2018) may also contribute to import.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citations to Wang et al., 2016.

claim: A Ran-independent nuclear import sequence in YAP/TAZ may contribute to import.
source: Furthermore, it is possible that Importin-alpha binding non-canonical nuclear import motifs within Yki (Wang et al., 2016) and a Ran-independent nuclear import sequence in YAP/TAZ (Kofler et al., 2018) may also contribute to import.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citation to Kofler et al., 2018.

claim: Non-canonical motifs in Yki and YAP/TAZ are not sufficient to maintain normal nuclear localisation of either Yki or YAP in the absence of Mask proteins.
source: However, these non-canonical motifs are not sufficient to maintain normal nuclear localisation of either Yki or YAP in the absence of Mask proteins.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing loss of nuclear localization in mask mutants.

claim: The Mask-Yki interaction must be weak and constitutive for Mask to promote nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling of Yki.
source: In order for Mask to promote nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling of Yki, the Mask-Yki interaction must be weak and constitutive – so that a pool of Yki protein is always dynamically shuttling.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed mechanism of Mask function.

claim: The regulation of the bulk distribution of Yki is determined by its choice of strong binding partner, namely either 14-3-3 in the cytoplasm or Sd in the nucleus.
source: The regulation of the bulk distribution of Yki is then determined simply by its choice of strong binding partner, namely either 14-3-3 in the cytoplasm or Sd in the nucleus, as mentioned above.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed mechanism of Yki regulation.

claim: There is always a 14-3-3 bound pool of Yki, a Sd bound pool of Yki and a third pool of Yki that can shuttle between the cytoplasm and nucleus by binding to Mask proteins and possibly other import/export factors.
source: Thus, there is always a 14-3-3 bound pool of Yki, a Sd bound pool of Yki and a third pool of Yki that can shuttle between the cytoplasm and nucleus by binding to Mask proteins and possibly other import/export factors.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed mechanism of Yki regulation.

claim: The relative proportions of the 14-3-3 bound and Sd bound pools determines the bulk distribution of Yki.
source: The relative proportions of the 14-3-3 bound and Sd bound pools determines the bulk distribution of Yki.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed mechanism of Yki regulation.

claim: Hippo signalling affects the 14-3-3 interaction by Yki phosphorylation.
source: Hippo signalling affects the 14-3-3 interaction (by Yki phosphorylation), while expression levels of the sd gene affects the Sd interaction.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of Hippo pathway regulation.

claim: Expression levels of the sd gene affects the Sd interaction with Yki.
source: Hippo signalling affects the 14-3-3 interaction (by Yki phosphorylation), while expression levels of the sd gene affects the Sd interaction.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed mechanism.

claim: There is no requirement for regulation of the Yki-Mask interaction.
source: According to this model, there is no requirement for regulation of the Yki-Mask interaction and we have no evidence for it.
evidence: This claim is based on the proposed model and lack of experimental evidence for regulation.

claim: Unlike Drosophila Yki, YAP/TAZ stability is regulated by two SCF-type E3 ubiquitin ligases, beta-TrCP and FBXW7.
source: Our findings also establish a novel role for mammalian Mask1/2 in stabilising YAP protein levels. Unlike Drosophila Yki, YAP/TAZ stability is regulated by two SCF-type E3 ubiquitin ligases, beta-TrCP and FBXW7, which earmark YAP/TAZ for degradation after phosphorylation by LATS and CK1 on a specific phosphodegron containing Ser381 (Tu et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tu et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2010.

claim: Beta-TrCP and FBXW7 earmark YAP/TAZ for degradation after phosphorylation by LATS and CK1 on a specific phosphodegron containing Ser381.
source: Our findings also establish a novel role for mammalian Mask1/2 in stabilising YAP protein levels. evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tu et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2010.

claim: Loss of Drosophila Mask does not reduce total Yki levels.
source: Consequently, while loss of Drosophila Mask does not reduce total Yki levels, loss of Mask1/2 causes a dramatic loss of YAP protein, suggesting that binding of Mask1/2 to YAP is essential to prevent YAP degradation.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observation comparing Drosophila and mammalian systems.

claim: Loss of Mask1/2 causes a dramatic loss of YAP protein.
source: Consequently, while loss of Drosophila Mask does not reduce total Yki levels, loss of Mask1/2 causes a dramatic loss of YAP protein, suggesting that binding of Mask1/2 to YAP is essential to prevent YAP degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Binding of Mask1/2 to YAP is essential to prevent YAP degradation.
source: Consequently, while loss of Drosophila Mask does not reduce total Yki levels, loss of Mask1/2 causes a dramatic loss of YAP protein, suggesting that binding of Mask1/2 to YAP is essential to prevent YAP degradation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that loss of Mask1/2 causes YAP protein loss.

claim: Similar YAP liquid droplets have been shown to occur by phase separation after treatment of cells expressing GFP-tagged YAP with 25% PEG to drive macromolecular crowding.
source: Similar YAP liquid droplets have recently been shown to occur by phase separation after treatment of cells expressing GFP-tagged YAP with 25% PEG to drive macromolecular crowding (Cai et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cai et al., 2018.

claim: Whether phase-separation of YAP has a physiological role is still unknown.
source: Whether phase-separation of YAP has a physiological role is still unknown, but the possibility is supported by our finding that endogenous YAP can also be observed to form droplets when in a complex with Mask1 at high concentrations.
evidence: This claim represents the current state of knowledge and is speculative.

claim: Endogenous YAP can be observed to form droplets when in a complex with Mask1 at high concentrations.
source: Whether phase-separation of YAP has a physiological role is still unknown, but the possibility is supported by our finding that endogenous YAP can also be observed to form droplets when in a complex with Mask1 at high concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Phase-separation has been proposed to support formation of transcriptional enhancer complexes ('transcription factories') in the nucleus.
source: Interestingly, phase-separation has been proposed to support formation of transcriptional enhancer complexes ('transcription factories') in the nucleus (Boehning et al., 2018; Boija et al., 2018; Hnisz et al., 2017; Iborra, 2007; Jackson et al., 1993; Lu et al., 2018; Sabari et al., 2018), and we speculate that Mask proteins might function in this manner to promote transcription.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Mask proteins might function to promote transcription through phase-separation.
source: Interestingly, phase-separation has been proposed to support formation of transcriptional enhancer complexes ('transcription factories') in the nucleus (Boehning et al., 2018; Boija et al., 2018; Hnisz et al., 2017; Iborra, 2007; Jackson et al., 1993; Lu et al., 2018; Sabari et al., 2018), and we speculate that Mask proteins might function in this manner to promote transcription.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation of droplet formation and citations to prior work on transcription factories.

claim: Mask family proteins contain a conserved RNA binding KH-domain.
source: Furthermore, Mask family proteins contain a conserved RNA binding KH-domain, and several RNA binding proteins have key roles in colloidal phase separation (Anderson and Kedersha, 2006; Lin et al., 2015; Maharana et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2011; Molliex et al., 2015; Ramaswami et al., 2013; Weber and Brangwynne, 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of Mask proteins shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mask family proteins contain two YAP-binding ankyrin repeat domains.
source: Finally, the fact that Mask family proteins contain two YAP-binding ankyrin repeat domains provides a plausible multivalent interaction mechanism by which Mask proteins could promote clustering of multiple YAP molecules in either the nucleus or cytoplasm, although further work is needed to explore this possibility (Figure 7D).

claim: Mask family proteins promote nuclear import of both Yki and YAP.
source: In conclusion, our results identify novel molecular mechanisms regulating the Yki/YAP/TAZ family of transcriptional co-activators. Mask family proteins promote nuclear import of both Yki and YAP, while also acting to stabilise YAP protein levels, which can lead to what appear to be YAP droplets at high concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mask family proteins act to stabilise YAP protein levels.
source: In conclusion, our results identify novel molecular mechanisms regulating the Yki/YAP/TAZ family of transcriptional co-activators. Mask family proteins promote nuclear import of both Yki and YAP, while also acting to stabilise YAP protein levels, which can lead to what appear to be YAP droplets at high concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Stabilisation of YAP protein levels by Mask proteins can lead to what appear to be YAP droplets at high concentrations.
source: In conclusion, our results identify novel molecular mechanisms regulating the Yki/YAP/TAZ family of transcriptional co-activators. Mask family proteins promote nuclear import of both Yki and YAP, while also acting to stabilise YAP protein levels, which can lead to what appear to be YAP droplets at high concentrations.

claim: Endogenous Mask1/2 and YAP co-localise in intracellular granules in both the nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: Endogenous Mask1/2 and YAP co-localise in intracellular granules in both the nucleus and cytoplasm, and the nucleo-cytoplasmic distribution of Mask1/2 and YAP is co-regulated in response to mechanical cues in human cells, most likely through direct association of the two proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: The nucleo-cytoplasmic distribution of Mask1/2 and YAP is co-regulated in response to mechanical cues in human cells.
source: Endogenous Mask1/2 and YAP co-localise in intracellular granules in both the nucleus and cytoplasm, and the nucleo-cytoplasmic distribution of Mask1/2 and YAP is co-regulated in response to mechanical cues in human cells, most likely through direct association of the two proteins.

claim: The co-regulation of Mask1/2 and YAP distribution is most likely through direct association of the two proteins.

claim: The functions of Mask family proteins are crucial to enable dynamic nuclear-cytoplasic shuttling and thus regulation of Yki/YAP/TAZ by Hippo signalling and Integrin signalling to control cellular behaviour.
source: These functions of Mask family proteins are crucial to enable dynamic nuclear-cytoplasic shuttling and thus regulation of these co-activators by Hippo signalling and Integrin signalling to control cellular behaviour.
